description.summary: Small, often invisible nature beings of Yucatec Maya tradition, regarded as guardians of the land, forest, and milpa (cornfield), capable of helping or harming humans depending on how they are treated.
description.full: An alux (Yucatec Maya [aˈluʃ], plural aluxo'ob) is a small, knee-high being of Yucatec Maya tradition, often described as resembling a miniature traditionally-dressed Maya person. Aluxo'ob are generally invisible but can take physical form to communicate or congregate. They are most strongly associated with the milpa (cornfield) and with caves and forests, and are regarded as guardians and as sources of mischief: they can call rain and protect crops, but if disrespected they will throw pots, blow out fires, hide tools, and bring sickness on those who offend them. Maya farmers traditionally build a small shelter (sometimes called a koben) for an alux when establishing a milpa, leaving offerings; after seven years the structure is sealed to prevent the being from running wild. Modern construction projects in the Yucatán, including the well-known Cancun Hyatt-area bridge, have included propitiatory rituals to the aluxo'ob to forestall accidents. The Yucatec aluxo'ob belong to a wider Mesoamerican family of small land spirits including the Nahuatl chanekeh / chaneque.

etymology.origin: From Yucatec Maya alux [aˈluʃ], plural aluxo'ob.
etymology.meaning: The word does not have an agreed external etymology; in tradition it simply names the being.
etymology.first_use: Documented in colonial-era and 20th-century Yucatec Maya ethnography.

features.description: Aluxo'ob are described as about knee-high to a person
When visible, resemble miniature Maya people in traditional clothing
Generally unseen; appear visibly when they choose to communicate

abilities.description: Default invisible state, with the option to appear visibly
Aluxo'ob bound to a milpa are said to summon rain and patrol the field at night to protect against thieves and pests
Throwing pots and pans, putting out fires, hiding tools, and other poltergeist-like phenomena when disrespected
Said to cause sickness in those who offend them or trespass on protected land

patterns: Bound to specific places, especially milpas and ruins
Respond to ritual offerings and respect
Active at night and at dawn

range.description: Yucatec Maya cultural area: the Yucatán Peninsula of Mexico, Belize, and northern Guatemala.

hotspots.name: Yucatán Peninsula
hotspots.notes: Aluxo'ob traditions are integral to milpa agriculture and ritual life across the peninsula.

first_recorded.source: Yucatec Maya oral and ritual tradition

peak_activity_periods.description: Aluxo'ob beliefs are continuously active in contemporary Maya communities

origins.cultural_roots: Yucatec Maya tradition; aluxo'ob are an integral part of agricultural ritual and land cosmology.
origins.earliest_accounts: Pre-Columbian Maya cosmology of small land beings (no direct surviving Classic-period text uses the word 'alux'); colonial and modern ethnography documents the tradition in detail.
origins.folklore_connections: Part of a wider Mesoamerican family of small nature spirits including the Nahuatl chanekeh.

timeline.event: Ethnographers document Yucatec aluxo'ob traditions and the milpa shelter / seven-year sealing custom
timeline.significance: Anchoring of the tradition in the academic record

history.modern_era: Aluxo'ob remain part of living Yucatec Maya practice. Construction firms working in the Yucatán routinely make ritual offerings to placate aluxo'ob; the practice has been widely reported in connection with Cancún-area projects.

paranormal.name: Genuine land spirits
paranormal.description: In Yucatec Maya tradition, aluxo'ob are real, sentient beings to whom respect and offerings are owed.

skeptical.name: Cultural personification of agricultural and ecological dynamics
skeptical.description: Aluxo'ob beliefs encode generations of ecological observation and risk management around the milpa, framed as relations with personified land beings.

traditions: Yucatec Maya milpa-shelter and seven-year tradition
stories: Aluxo'ob aiding farmers who treat them respectfully
Aluxo'ob causing illness or disturbance to disrespectful trespassers
folklore.beliefs: Aluxo'ob are owed respect, offerings, and proper ritual; they are not invoked frivolously.

indigenous.significance: Aluxo'ob are part of living Maya cosmology and agricultural practice, not merely 'folklore' in the antiquarian sense.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: Aluxo'ob beliefs are an active religious / ritual tradition; representations should respect the source community.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: Use Yucatec Maya sources where possible; avoid trivialising the tradition by treating aluxo'ob purely as 'fairies' or game characters.

other: Construction-site propitiation ceremonies in Cancún and the Riviera Maya

research.ongoing_studies: Active ethnographic interest in Yucatec Maya cosmology and agricultural ritual.
